opus-5.5.text:
I think there's a lot of value there, but it's important to be precise about where that value comes in. My background is mostly in reinforcement learning for locomotion and low-level control, so training policies in simulation that let legged robots walk, climb, and recover from pushes. For that kind of problem, you don't really need a huge model. You need a fast, robust controller running at high frequency on the robot, and a relatively small network trained with massive amounts of simulated experience works remarkably well.

But once you move to more abstract tasks, like "go find the toolbox in the other room and bring it to me," the challenge isn't how to move your legs. It's understanding the scene, reasoning about what the person wants, breaking that into steps, and handling situations you've never seen. That's where large models, vision-language models in particular, bring something we simply couldn't get before. They carry a lot of common-sense knowledge about the world that you'd never be able to hand-engineer or learn from robot data alone.

So the way I see it, you end up with a hierarchy. At the top, a large model handles semantic understanding and high-level planning, at a slower rate. At the bottom, you still have these specialized, efficient controllers handling the dynamics and contact at hundreds of hertz. The interesting research question is the interface between the two: what's the right abstraction to pass down? Waypoints, skills, latent commands? And how do you make the low-level policies general enough that the high-level model can actually rely on them?

There's also a push toward more end-to-end approaches, where a single big model outputs actions directly, and I think that's promising for manipulation especially. But for dynamic tasks on legged robots, the latency and reliability requirements are tough. So in the near term I expect a combination: large models for the "what" and "why," and learned controllers from simulation for the "how." Over time those boundaries will probably blur as models get faster and we get more robot data.

r001.rationale: The response says larger models help with abstract tasks involving reasoning and breaking tasks into steps, but it does not state that these tasks require orchestrating actions over multiple minutes.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think it's important to separate what the large models are actually good at from what we need for low-level control. The locomotion work we've done with legged robots, the ANYmal stuff, that's all small networks. A few layers, very fast, trained with reinforcement learning in simulation. And the reason they're small is that the problem is actually pretty narrow once you frame it right: you have proprioceptive observations, maybe some terrain information, and you need to output joint targets at hundreds of hertz. You don't need a billion parameters for that, and honestly you don't want them, because you need the inference to run on the robot's onboard compute with very tight latency.

Where I see the large models being valuable is one level up. If you want the robot to do something abstract, like "go check whether the door on the second floor is closed," there's a lot of semantic understanding there that we have no good way of getting from reinforcement learning alone. The reward would be impossible to specify. So the natural division is that the large model, whether that's a language model or a vision-language model, handles the high-level reasoning, decomposes the task, understands the scene, and then it calls into these learned low-level skills that we already know how to train robustly.

What I find interesting is the interface between the two. Right now it's often quite crude, the big model outputs a waypoint or picks from a library of skills. I think the more interesting question is whether you can make that interface richer, so the high-level model can actually shape how the low-level controller behaves, say, "move carefully here because the surface looks slippery," without having to retrain anything. We're starting to see some of that, and I think it's where a lot of the practical value will come from, rather than trying to make one enormous end-to-end model that does everything from pixels to torques. That might work eventually, but the data requirements are brutal, and you lose the thing that made the simulation-based approach so effective, which is that you can generate essentially unlimited experience for the low-level problem.

astra-6.text:
I think the value is in connecting an abstract instruction to something the robot can actually execute. If you tell a robot, “Clean up this room,” that leaves a lot unspecified. It has to understand what you mean, break that down into smaller tasks, and decide which skills to use. Larger models can help at that level.

But you still need reliable skills underneath. Understanding that you should pick up an object doesn’t mean you can control the robot well enough to do it. So I see a lot of potential in combining that higher-level reasoning with policies that handle the physical interaction. The important connection is making sure the plan is grounded in what the robot can actually do.

r001.rationale: The response says larger models can turn abstract instructions into subtasks and select skills, but it does not state that these tasks involve orchestrating actions over multiple minutes.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the value is in connecting an abstract instruction to something the robot can actually execute. If you say, “Clean up the kitchen,” there are a lot of decisions hidden in that request. You have to understand what needs to move, where it belongs, and which actions to take first. Larger models can help with that kind of reasoning and with interpreting what the robot sees.

But there’s still a gap between describing an action and executing it reliably. A model might tell the robot to pick up a cup, but that doesn’t automatically give it the ability to grasp the cup or maintain its balance while reaching for it. So I see a useful combination: a larger model handles the more abstract decisions, and lower-level policies provide the physical skills. The important question is how to connect those levels so that the plan reflects what the robot can actually do.
